droppedAngles.title: silent-drops
droppedAngles.why: Traced body.name directly through the route into exportTransfers, path.join, writeFile, and the JSON response; it does not pass through Store, SCHEMA, an ORM, or another filtering persistence layer.

droppedAngles.title: migrations-and-rollout
droppedAngles.why: The diff changes no schema, stored record shape, migration, persisted ledger data, or compatibility path between deployed versions.

scoutNotes: The PR lets an authenticated account owner provide an optional export filename, returns the resulting basename, and retains the account-derived default. It also adds a warning on failed requireUser authentication containing request and authorization data.

confirmed.title: Failed sign-ins leak credentials
confirmed.rootCause: Failed-authentication logging emits the complete Authorization header, exposing bearer credentials contrary to the logging contract.
confirmed.summary: Failed-authentication logging exposes the complete Authorization header and raw request URL. Although trailing HTTP whitespace is normalized and does not trigger the failure, other valid malformed header values can contain an active bearer token and are logged verbatim.
confirmed.failure: GET /accounts?access_token=query-secret with Authorization: Bearer tok-bob extra reaches the real server, returns 401, and logs ["sign-in failed","GET","/accounts?access_token=query-secret","with","Bearer tok-bob extra"], exposing the active reusable token tok-bob and the query secret.
confirmed.reasoning: src/server.js passes the real IncomingMessage to requireUser, and src/auth.js logs req.headers.authorization and req.url without redaction whenever authenticate returns null. The existing authentication contract explicitly says tokens are never logged. Through the running HTTP server, the cited trailing-space header was normalized to "Bearer tok-bob", authenticated successfully with status 200, and produced no warning. However, a reachable request using Authorization: "Bearer tok-bob extra" returned 401 and captured console.warn arguments containing both "Bearer tok-bob extra" and "/accounts?access_token=query-secret". Thus the cited input is inaccurate, but the credential and query-string disclosure is real. The full test suite passed and contains no assertion preventing this disclosure. The parent commit lacked this logging, confirming the diff introduced it.
confirmed.panel: 3 of 3 skeptics could not refute it

confirmed.title: Named exports escape export directory
confirmed.rootCause: The caller-controlled export name is joined to exportDir without basename or containment validation, allowing path traversal outside the authorized directory.
confirmed.summary: Joining an untrusted name without enforcing a basename lets authenticated callers write or overwrite CSV files outside exportDir.
confirmed.failure: An authenticated account owner can submit {"name":"../escaped"}; the server returns 200 while writeFile creates escaped.csv outside exportDir. On Windows, "..\\escaped" has the equivalent effect.
confirmed.reasoning: The authenticated export route accepts any nonempty string up to 64 characters and passes it unchanged to exportTransfers. No basename or containment check intervenes. An end-to-end request using name "../escaped" returned 200 with file "escaped.csv" and created escaped.csv beside the export directory. Node's Windows path semantics likewise treat backslash traversal as directory traversal.

confirmed.title: Concurrent saves commit failed transfers
confirmed.rootCause: Concurrent Store.save calls use the same process-scoped temporary filename, so their writes and renames race and can produce a failure response after data was committed.
confirmed.summary: All concurrent saves share the same process-scoped temporary filename, allowing a committed mutation to receive a failure response.
confirmed.failure: Two concurrent valid transfers can both be persisted while one request receives 500 because the other save already renamed their shared temporary file. Retrying the reported failure applies another transfer.
confirmed.reasoning: Store.save uses ledger.json.<pid>.tmp for every save and has no serialization or unique suffix. A concurrent HTTP probe reproduced the race on its first attempt: two 10-cent transfers returned statuses [201,500], the failed request logged ENOENT while renaming the shared temporary file, and the persisted ledger contained both memos with the source balance reduced from 100 to 80. Retrying the apparent failure would create another transfer because the endpoint has no idempotency mechanism. The PR does not modify Store.save, so the finding is correctly classified as pre-existing.

confirmed.title: Named exports overwrite across accounts
confirmed.rootCause: Named exports share one global filename namespace and writeFile replaces existing files, allowing accounts and users to overwrite one another's exports.
confirmed.summary: Caller-supplied names create a process-wide shared namespace where one account's export silently overwrites another's.
confirmed.failure: Owners of different accounts can choose the same valid export name. The later successful export silently replaces the earlier user's CSV in the shared export directory.
confirmed.reasoning: Authorization limits which account is exported but does not partition export filenames by account or user. Every request writes path.join(exportDir, name + ".csv") with writeFile replacement semantics. An end-to-end probe exported Bob's transfer to shared.csv and then exported Cy's account under the same name; both returned 200, and afterward the file contained Cy's transfer ID but no longer Bob's.

confirmed.title: Named exports grow storage unbounded
confirmed.rootCause: Arbitrary persistent export names can create an unlimited number of full CSV files because there is no quota, retention policy, or cleanup mechanism.
confirmed.summary: Each distinct valid name permanently creates another full CSV without a quota, retention policy, or cleanup path.
confirmed.failure: An authenticated owner can repeatedly export the same account under distinct names, accumulating full persistent CSV copies. On a filesystem shared with the ledger, exhausting its capacity makes subsequent exports and ledger saves return 500.
confirmed.reasoning: Each distinct valid name selects a distinct persistent path, writeFile creates it, and the repository contains no quota, retention, deletion, or cleanup path for exports. A probe issued twelve exports named copy-0 through copy-11 and observed twelve files. Exports contain the account's complete CSV, and an ENOSPC error from either export writeFile or Store.save propagates to the server's generic 500 handler.

confirmed.title: Accepted names can create no file
confirmed.rootCause: Length-only name validation accepts filesystem-invalid or reserved filenames, including embedded NULs and Windows device names, causing errors or unintended device writes.
confirmed.summary: The length-only validation accepts names that are not portable filenames, causing internal errors or writes to Windows devices instead of creating a CSV.
confirmed.failure: An authenticated owner can submit a name containing U+0000 and receive a 500 instead of a validation error; on Windows, reserved device names such as NUL are also accepted. Path separators additionally permit writes outside the configured export directory.

sites.title: Accepted names can create no file

confirmed.reasoning: The authenticated export route passes any 1–64 character string directly into path.join and writeFile. A focused request with {"name":"bad\u0000name"} reached writeFile and returned 500 with ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE. Microsoft’s naming rules also confirm that NUL.csv is the reserved NUL device on Windows. Additionally, {"name":"../escaped"} returned 200 and created escaped.csv outside the export directory.

confirmed.title: Warnings expose query-string secrets
confirmed.rootCause: Failed-authentication logging records req.url instead of the parsed pathname, exposing query-string secrets and making the logged path unstable.
confirmed.summary: The warning records raw req.url rather than the parsed pathname, so arbitrary query values are exposed and make the promised path field unstable.
confirmed.failure: GET /accounts?access_token=query-secret with Authorization: Bearer guessed-secret returns 401 and logs both /accounts?access_token=query-secret and Bearer guessed-secret rather than only the parsed pathname.
confirmed.reasoning: A focused unauthenticated GET to /accounts?access_token=query-secret produced a warning containing the complete raw URL. The same warning also contained the complete Authorization header, contradicting auth.js's existing statement that tokens are never logged.

confirmed.title: Body errors bypass sign-in warnings
confirmed.rootCause: POST bodies are parsed before route authentication runs, so malformed or oversized unauthenticated requests bypass the failed-sign-in warning.
confirmed.summary: Protected POST requests are parsed before requireUser runs, so malformed or oversized bodies suppress the failed-sign-in event entirely.
confirmed.failure: POST /accounts with Authorization: Bearer guessed-secret and body "{" returns 400 body must be JSON without recording a failed-sign-in warning.
confirmed.reasoning: server.js resolves the route and awaits readJson before invoking the requireUser-wrapped handler. In a focused run, malformed JSON with an invalid bearer token returned 400 and emitted no warning; the same request with valid JSON reached requireUser, returned 401, and emitted the warning.

confirmed.title: Exports omit actor attribution
confirmed.rootCause: Export creation and replacement do not append an audit record identifying the authenticated actor.
confirmed.summary: The authenticated export write creates or overwrites a file without recording the acting user's identity in the audit trail.
confirmed.failure: After an authenticated user creates or replaces an export CSV, the audit collection and persisted ledger contain no export event identifying that user.
confirmed.reasoning: exportTransfers writes the CSV, but neither it nor the route calls record or store.save. In a focused run, opening an account created one audit entry, and a successful named export created statement.csv while the audit count remained one. The parent commit has the same omission for account-named exports, including replacement on repeated exports, so the finder correctly classified it as pre-existing.

confirmed.title: Unicode characters are miscounted
confirmed.rootCause: The advertised character limit is enforced with JavaScript string.length, which counts UTF-16 code units rather than Unicode characters.
confirmed.summary: Using string.length enforces UTF-16 code units rather than the advertised number of characters.
confirmed.failure: Posting `{ "name": "😀" repeated 40 times }` to an owned account's export route returns 400 even though the supplied name contains only 40 Unicode code points.
confirmed.reasoning: The authenticated HTTP route is reachable and validates `name.length` directly at src/server.js:103. A focused request with 40 grinning-face characters produced 40 Unicode code points but 80 UTF-16 code units and returned 400 with `name must be 1 to 64 characters`. The added test covers only an ASCII 65-character boundary and does not prevent this failure.

confirmed.title: Null request bodies crash exports
confirmed.rootCause: The export handler destructures body without verifying it is a non-null object, so a JSON null body causes an internal error.
confirmed.summary: The handler destructures the parsed body without ensuring that the JSON root is an object.
confirmed.failure: Posting the valid JSON body `null` to an owned account's export route throws while destructuring `body` and returns 500 instead of a client validation error.
confirmed.reasoning: `readJson` returns `JSON.parse(...)` without restricting the root type, and the authenticated export handler executes `const { name } = body`. Through the real HTTP server, posting JSON `null` to an owned account produced the cited TypeError at src/server.js:102 and returned 500 `{ "error": "internal error" }`. No caller, parser guard, or test prevents it.

confirmed.title: Reported surrogate filename is untrue
confirmed.rootCause: Unpaired UTF-16 surrogates are accepted and returned verbatim even though filesystem encoding substitutes U+FFFD, making the reported filename inaccurate.
confirmed.summary: An unpaired UTF-16 surrogate is accepted and returned verbatim even though filesystem encoding replaces it with U+FFFD.
confirmed.failure: Exporting with a name containing lone U+D800 returns `\ud800.csv`, but the created directory entry is `�.csv`, so the reported filename differs from the filename present on disk.
confirmed.reasoning: The route accepts a one-code-unit string containing lone U+D800, passes it into `path.join`, and returns `path.basename(file)` from the pre-encoding JavaScript string. A real HTTP export returned 200 with a response filename whose first code unit was 55296, while `readdir` showed `�.csv` whose first code point was 65533. Thus filesystem path encoding changed the name after the value used for the response was formed.

missed.what: src/export.js removes path.basename from the unnamed-export fallback, so an account ID containing path components can now escape the export directory even when no name is supplied.
missed.why: The reported traversal finding covers the new request-controlled name. It does not cover the separate regression in exportTransfers' existing three-argument contract or account IDs loaded directly from persisted data; the stated promise that unnamed exports behave “as before” is therefore false.
